title: Two bullets and a Taser couldn't take Welton down
article: It took two bullets and two hits from a Taser to take Derek Welton down the night he died, a B.C. Coroners inquest has revealed.
The inquest, which began Monday in Duncan, marks the first time the public has heard details surrounding Welton's death.
Welton, a known drug user with a history of violence, was killed by police March 1, 2009.
RCMP had arrived at Welton's Boys Road trailer that evening in response to an abandoned 911 call from the 39-year-old's cellphone.
Audio recordings of Welton's conversations with 911 dispatchers were played for presiding coroner Rodrick MacKenzie and a four-man, three-woman jury.
The first call, made at 5:35 p.m., included Welton screaming "I need protection" before the call was disconnected.
The first RCMP officer, Const. Greg Bouvier, arrived at Welton's home at 5:51 p.m. and found Welton had locked his trailer door and would not come out despite repeated requests.
Meanwhile, Welton had dialed 911 again because of the police presence at his door. Hesaid he was "scared to death" because the police had beaten him up "so many times."
At first, he told the dispatcher he was unarmed, but then became agitated and said he was arming himself and shouted, "and they're going to have to fucking shoot me" before the call was disconnected.
The officers explained at the inquest they had wanted to apprehend Welton under the Mental Health Act and take him to the hospital for treatment.
Welton eventually unlocked the door for Cpl. Greg Pask, who was serving as watch commander during March 1's day shift. was asked to attend the scene.
Pask was followed inside by Const. Kara Gelech -- who is trained to use a Taser -- and Cpl. Bob Purslow.
Welton was standing in the kitchen at the back of the trailer, within arm's reach of two long, carving knives.
Pask asked to Welton to step away from the knives, to come and sit at the table so the two could talk.
Welton, Pask said, told him he'd been wronged by BC hydro, and seemed agitated when talking about an ex-girlfriend.
Meanwhile, Gelech had decided to utilize the "element of surprise" and deployed her Taser to stun and apprehend Welton.
Instead, she said as he began to fall Welton sprung up "almost like a cat," grabbed the knives and ran at the police swinging the blades "like a windmill."
As Purslow and Gelech started to exit the trailer, Pask said he thought first of exiting too, but saw the door was blocked by the two officers. At that point, Pask fired his first shot at Welton.
He said it "did not appear to have any effect at all."
Seeing his exit was still blocked, Pask fired again. He said Welton appeared to feel some effect from the shot, but continued to attack.
Pask fired his third and final shot and left the trailer.
Two of the three shots actually hit Welton.
Moments later, three officers went back into the trailer but Welton continued to fight, and the police struggled to get him into handcuffs so that they could allow waiting ambulance attendants in.
That's when Gelech deployed her Taser a second time.
She said Welton stiffened, went down to the ground and again tried to reach his knives, but she grabbed them first and took them out of the trailer.
Welton was taken by ambulance to Cowichan District Hospital, but was pronounced dead at 7:40 p.m.
Police at the inquest mulled the possibility Welton was experiencing excited delirium.

According to the American College of Emergency Physicians, excited delirium includes insensitivity to pain and superhuman strength and is sometimes associated with the use police restraint and Tasers. It most commonly occurs in male subjects with a history of mental illness and/or chronic drug abuse, particularly cocaine -- Welton's drug of choice.

The inquest, which continues today and Thursday, is not a fault-finding investigation but rather an opportunity for the seven-member jury to make recommendations aimed at preventing deaths under similar circumstances in the future.
No criminal charges have been recommended for Pask or the other officers involved after a lengthy police investigation.
Participating in the inquest are David Kwan, counsel for the RCMP, and attorney Mike Coleman on behalf of Welton's father, Carroll.
